newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ economic slowdown may be longer, says HSBC.
newsitem.headline: NZ economic slowdown may be longer, says HSBC.

text.p: The slowdown that started in the New Zealand economy in the March quarter has the potential to be deeper and longer than expected, according to a report by Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation.
In the three months to the end of March the economy fell back by a worse-than-expected 0.5 percent, the New Zealand Press Association reports.
The report says the economy's rate of growth has been slowing since March 1993 and showed initial signs of bottoming out in early 1995.
Growth since the end of December had averaged 2.6 percent, with most market players expecting the economy would grow in the March quarter.
But economic growth stalled and that prompted the Reserve Bank to relax monetary policy by 100 basis points at the end of June.

The Hongkong Bank report says the slowdown may be worse than expected. It points out that weekly M3, a broad measure of money in the economy, has fallen substantially and risks shrinking further in coming weeks.
M3 is a good indicator of inflation and economic activity. Since July last year, M3 has shown a consistent decline, the report says.
Reserve Bank figures issued on yesterday showed M3 at $83.3 billion at June 25, up just 1.3 percent from the same week a year before. In the two previous weeks, growth in M3 was 0.3 and 0.2 percent.
M3 measures all currency and total deposits with trading banks, plus deposits with all savings banks.
Both weekly and monthly M3 levels went sharply backwards in the recession in 1991, Hongkong Bank says.
"While monthly M3 still looks relatively healthy, weekly M3 figures are typically a good indication of where the figures will trend towards," the report says.
The continuation of the downward trend and the possibility M3 may shrink "is a concern for the health of the economy".

"Any further decline from these levels may signal a deeper and longer slowdown than many commentators are willing to admit, and even a recession during the March to September quarters of 1997," the report says.
Monetary conditions, the mix of interest rates and the dollar have eased since December, but the economy continues to show signs that it has not yet bottomed out.

Those signs included the 0.5 percent fall in gross domestic product in the March quarter, the rise in unemployment from 5.9 percent to 6.4 percent over the March quarter and a fall in building consents since March.

Exporters and manufacturers are still finding conditions difficult. For example wool exports were down 12 percent in the year to April, and wood pulp exports were down more than a quarter in the same period.
